newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-WHITAKER, DE LA HOYA OUT FOR "POUND-FOR-POUND" CROWN.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-WHITAKER, DE LA HOYA OUT FOR "POUND-FOR-POUND" CROWN.

text.p: Pernell Whitaker and Oscar De La Hoya tangle for the World Boxing Council welterweight title on Saturday with each of the former Olympic gold medalists hoping to emerge from the fight heralded as the world's best boxer, pound-for-pound.
And the mythical title appears to be every bit as much on the minds of those connected with the eagerly-anticipated bout as the real crown that Whitaker will defend at the Thomas and Mack Arena.

"For the last 10 years he has been the best pound-for-pound fighter in the world," De La Hoya's promoter, Bob Arum, said of the 33-year-old Whitaker. "He has done nothing but win and win in spectacular fashion."
Arum, however, thinks his 24-year-old rising star is about to stake a claim to the unoffical title that spurs the most passionate debates among fight fans.
"Oscar De La Hoya has had a meteoric career. He has fought all the best in his weight categories and now he stands on the threshhold being the best pound-for-pound fighter there is," Arum said.
Whitaker (40-1-1) will be making the ninth defence of his WBC welterweight crown, one of six world titles he has picked up in a stellar professional career.

The 1984 Olympic champion also has owned at one time or another the WBC, World Boxing Association and International Boxing Federation lightweight titles, the IBF junior welterweight crown and the WBA junior middleweight belt.

De La Hoya, who takes an unblemished 23-0 record into the ring, at 24 has already won the IBF lightweight and WBC junior welterweight crowns before moving up to challenge for Whitaker's welterweight title.
"I want to be the best fighter in the history of boxing," said De La Hoya of his rather lofty aspirations.

"It's part of my goal to capture world titles in six different weight classes. This fight gets me a little closer. He's just another opponent I have to beat," said De La Hoya, the lone American boxer to emerge from the 1992 Barcelona Olympics with a gold medal.
"Winning six titles is creating history. That's how they will know me forever," added the popular De La Hoya, who is expected to earn $10 million -- $3 million more than the champion.
Sugar Ray Leonard and Thomas Hearns share the record for winning titles in five different weight classes.
De La Hoya handles fans and the media -- fielding questions in English and Spanish with equal ease -- with such aplomb that it belies his relative inexperience.
"He's a fighter who knows this part of it is as important as what you do inside the ring," Arum said. "(Sugar Ray) Leonard wasn't as natural as this kid.
"I think he'll be the best fighter of all time," added Arum, raising the hype level a notch or two.
But Whitaker's slick style has befuddled a long list of opponents and he has been waiting for a mega-fight like this since his controversial draw with Julio Cesar Chavez in 1993.

Unlike De La Hoya, Whitaker does not appear to be particularly interested in commercial endorsements or a future film career. Like his charismatic opponent, however, Whitaker is concerned with his place in boxing history and the recognition that would come from a victory Saturday.
"This is the fight I'm going to be remembered for," Whitaker predicted.
